text: Hello, everyone. Welcome to the UniAxis, and this time we have the Ashoka University with us. So, we have Anju Jayaraj from Ashoka University. Over to you, Anju.

Thanks, Vijaya. Hi, good evening, everyone. Hi, Anu. My god, so many people that I'm... I'm also meeting, I think, a lot of people from TOC after a long time. Apart from the regular meetups that we do. Just as an introduction, my name is Anju. I head the Office of Outreach at Ashoka. And unfortunately, today, due to a personal emergency, I don't have Morsha joining me for the session. So, I thought I'll just quickly take you through what we've been doing, the kind of program that we have, but I think a little more deep dive on the admissions bit as to how we view it, what are our goals coming up in the, you know, next few years. I don't have a slide, I think, on one of the new additions that we had this year, but we can talk about it. I don't want it to be a one-way presentation as such. I think I say this in all of my presentations that I hate doing presentations. So, as—as much as we can, you know, whatever the—your questions are, I'd love to take them as—as many as possible as well. Let's look this through. Vijaya, we can move on. Or do you want me to wait for a bit?
Yeah, I think we can get going.

Okay. Cool. I think this is... liberal education is a framework. And when I talk to counselors also on a day-to-day basis, I realize that our understanding of liberal education is very different from one person to the other. For us at Ashoka, over the last, what, 12 years now, 12, 14 years that we've been, you know, progressing in this particular framework, for us, the concept of liberal education essentially lies in the fact that any and every particular subject, or like people like to confuse with say, liberal arts being only something that is very skewed towards humanities, skewed towards social sciences, and that's why I think on a very regular basis we keep getting feedback that, "Oh yeah, you should look at Ashoka for say, social sciences." Or "You should look at Ashoka for say, humanities," or something of—of, you know, on those lines. I would like to bring this to everyone's fore that liberal arts particularly also means just free knowledge, and there's nothing else to do with, you know, particularly the field of arts or anything else that we would like to, you know, assume about it. So essentially, our entire curriculum is based in the fact that students need to access a very interdisciplinary way of education. The education has to be something that gives them the freedom to go ahead and pick out subjects or pick out areas that they can seem to maybe have possible connections with, and then be able to sort of bring out outcomes. I—I'd just like to focus on a couple of things that we're seeing in, you know, within the job market, within also how higher academic options are—have been sort of looking at Ashokan students. There is a core appreciation. So, while at Ashoka, for those of you who may also know, we have an active cohort of students that is picked up by the best of organizations every year, and these are organizations that span across multiple disciplines, right? So, consulting, we're very strong. So, you will have a McKinsey, you will have a Google, you will have multiple other spaces, product companies. Similarly, development, in fact, I was just talking to someone just about yesterday on—on, you know, how the placement trends have been this year. And what's surprising to us is that we're seeing a massive uptick in students at Ashoka, in their final years, picking up careers which are very impact-driven. Careers which are very, you know, we'd like to call it that if you want to do something which is very impactful in the society, then the thought process is ki aap jhola lagake fir chale jaoge. You're—you're working in a particular space jahan pe shayad paisa nahi milega, or you're working in organizations where, essentially, they're not really funded very well in terms of salaries and otherwise. But we're seeing an uptick in—in terms of demand for such roles, having said that, within a particular corporate setup. So, while consulting is a field that we know every particular student at Ashoka vies for, we're also looking at a lot of development consulting roles that have come up in the past few years with various organizations, whether it's the CSR departments, whether it is, you know, policy, governance. And the kind of students that they pick up is, very surprisingly, without a trend. So, it's not that, okay, only an economic student will get something of that sort or only a student from say, maybe economics and finance or maybe political sciences or any of those particular spaces will get a certain kind of job. It is essentially the skill that students bring in to, which focuses on the fact that you can draw upon the narrative which is, whether it is natural sciences, whether it's a narrative of sciences, mathematics, humanities. I was—you know, we were going through a couple of projects the other day where there are students wanting to build a career, or rather a—a particular space for themselves, within food and within cooking, particularly, as a space where they want to build more—more and more, you know, dishes for people to go ahead and sample. But the way that they are curating these dishes is more based on chemistry, is more based on their inputs that they've learnt in from different other spaces, how we could use that particular lens. So, I think that's what we stand for at Ashoka. It's never been that someone needs to come in with a—it's not a mandate for someone to come in with a very focused mindset that this is the way that, you know, I want to go ahead and pick up my academic career, pursue an academic career in one particular discipline. We'd like them to be very curious about different disciplines. And therefore, an interdisciplinary approach, how do you sort of sample that particular breadth and depth in your curriculum, that becomes very important for students who are coming into Ashoka, or who we'd like to pick at Ashoka as well. Vijaya, we can move on.

So, just to give you a gist of students who may not be... if—if we are on the previous slide. And the previous slide, and the previous slide. Yeah, this one right there. At Ashoka right now, as it is with the NEP, the National Education Policy, we have all of our programs are four-year programs, between... so, students can pursue them as a BA, BSc honors, or they can pursue them as a BA, BSc honors with research. So, depends on the components that they want to pick up in their courses. And naturally, these particular courses include their foundation courses, majors, minors, co-curriculars, all of these particular aspects come into picture. It's academically rigorous. So, naturally, we are also looking at students who have the academic acumen to be able to, let's say, succeed within those four years of programs, you know. We—we often get questions, both Morsha and I, that what is it that you look for or when you're selecting a student, is there a certain way that you're evaluating that child? I think for us it's very clear. It does not depend so much on the academic prowess that is shown on the marksheet, but it depends a lot on what is the academic mindset that the child has. At the end of the day, the child is entering into a four-year life journey where it's built up with students and peers who are extremely curious, who are experimental, they'd like to go ahead, they are—they like taking initiatives to go ahead and sample courses that they've never probably, you know, dabbled in. And if someone misses that curiosity bit, no matter how academically strong they might be otherwise in their profile, we see that the fitment may not be right with Ashoka. So, we also advise the student to look at colleges which might be a little different for them. And I think that fitment is very important. But having said that, these are rigorous programs. And all of our students, and I'm mentioning this because I'll come a little bit later when we talk about admissions in detail, all of our particular students, irrespective of what backgrounds and what particular majors they want to look at, what subjects they want to look at, all of these particular students have to go through their foundation courses. There are nine of them, uh, that the students go ahead and finish in the first three, two, three semesters. Similarly, the kind of majors that they want to pick up, you can build up your academic profile at Ashoka with a bunch of elective courses or a bunch of independent modules, or you could just focus on one major and a one, you know, one particular minor and then take it up the route that you want to sort of go ahead for. Research is a very, very strong part of Ashoka. And I think, again, is one of the skills that we look at admissions. So, if you—if you look at the structure of the course here, when we look at foundation programs and, Vijaya, if you can just move to the next slide once. Now, the nine foundation courses that you see, these obviously are skill-oriented, right? And these are courses that go ahead and sort of are applicable across any discipline that they wish to pursue, academic or professional, any particular situation that they go ahead and deal with. These are the kind of skills that they will have to employ at any particular perspective. Now, when I'm looking at critical thinking or when I'm looking at mind and behavior, which focuses on how you're thinking, how your perception is about, how your awareness level is about things around you. These are also the kind of questions or these are also the basis of the kind of questions that students get asked when we're looking at their application forms. So, look at the application form, if, you know, a lot of you have counseled students for Ashoka, and you may be aware that our application form has a question on what are the kind of books that you read. Now, for me, that reading ability is extremely important because if the student does not have a reading habit, or does not have a very strong understanding of how to browse through large—large particular texts, then for them it might be difficult for them to also be on campus and actually compete with other students. So, when I'm looking at great books, that's a course that builds into that. Similarly, critical thinking we teach, I don't expect a student to be at this stage very critical-thinking oriented, although a lot of schools are doing a fantastic job, and we do get students who are very self-aware and who know how they're thinking through. But at the same time, for us, I think the—rather what we're looking at is, how does a particular student actually think in a situation. So, we look that through through the personal essays, through what is the other profiles that they've actually mentioned. So, everything in the admission process also draws in from the kind of curriculum course that we have, whether it's foundational, whether it is something else. If someone has mentioned that they're extremely passionate about a field and that's the field that they want to pursue, so someone's very passionate about economics or passionate about pol science, and that's why they're coming to Ashoka, then of course, the expectation is that they know a lot more about these subjects outside of what is only taught, you know, in classes. So, is there a format that students can, you know, build themselves? I—I was asked this question by a student from a particular school very recently that, "Anju, can you just give me the framework, you know? What are the things that I need to do, and I will get into Ashoka? So, what kind of, what do you say, what kind of, what kind of social work do I do? What kind of extracurricular activities do I do? Can I do these five things? And do you think Ashoka will take me?" It doesn't work like that. It's very contextual, and it draws in from this. So, our advice to students also is usually, and to counselors as well, is when you're starting off and you're starting off a little early on, it is always better for students to also familiarize themselves with the entire curriculum structure. Now, all of these courses are given in detail on the website. The foundation courses, what happens in a major, what kind of programs will they study, what kind of courses will they study, what are the research papers that they may have to go through. And you get this information on multiple spaces, not just the website, even if you talk to an alum or a current student at Ashoka, you will be able to access this. Familiarize yourself with this ecosystem first before actually attempting the application as such. Once you're familiar with this, you know what is the narrative that you want to build for yourself in that application form. Or which actually sits down. Maybe there's something in Indian civilizations that really catches your eye, and you think that this can help me build a career in, let's say, analytics within the social development sector. If there is something that you can draw in from that, it's wonderful because then we know that you're curious, you're also very open-minded in terms of how you've researched upon the university, what is your intention when you're coming in, and how you can draw upon that. Vijaya, we can go to the next one.

For pure majors, of course, there are a bunch of majors that are there in total right now, I think, 27, 28, I've stopped keeping track of it. But yes, students can pursue science majors, pure science majors, which are with biochemistry, CS, CS and AI, math, physics. We've also introduced a bunch of new courses this year. Uh, management this year, we saw a massive uptick in students who picked up management as a preferred major, the incoming cohort that comes in tomorrow. Uh, at the same time, you know, our traditional courses like psychology or international relations or economics, for that matter, they've always been. All of these pure majors that you see on your screen right now, except for computer sciences and AI, as of now, can be taken as a minor, which means that a student will have the combination. So, someone picks up say, uh, management major, could also do maybe a math minor because they think that it's—it sort of syncs in really well, or a history minor because "I want to build something, uh, you know, within history and management together." So, either ways, all of these majors that you see on your screen, all of these can also be taken as a minor. It totally depends on how the student wants to marry their particular, uh, you know, academic aspirations within the particular program. Go ahead, please.

In terms of interdisciplinary majors again, uh, bunch of them. The Comp Science, Math and Economics is a new one that we've introduced this year. Uh, you could sort of look at them. You can look at Economics and History. We don't have Art History as of now, uh, as a subject, I think there's a question on the chat box. Not as of now as a major, but yes, there are students who pick up a History major and then combine an Art minor in case if they wish to, you know, pursue something on—on those particular aspects. Or they could take an English and Performing Arts major. So, all of these particular majors are available to any particular student. There are some courses, I think in the previous slide you would have seen some of these courses have an asterisk on them. They have subject-specific requirements. Uh, you may need a math in your grade 11 and grade 12. You may need, if you don't have a math and then you suddenly decide— humanities student suddenly decides after one and a half years that they want to do a CS major, uh, you will have to take care of certain prerequisite courses, get a certain grade. There is a grade requirement in all of those particular subjects for you to be able to take the computer science program or any other program that has a, uh, subject-specific requirement as such. So, those aspects will be there, but essentially, these are not tied to a certain discipline that students have taken in their class 11th and 12th. You could pick them up across any background, any particular field. I also feel that this kind of an education gives a lot of space for students, and specifically in India, uh, to sort of look at, and I'm—I—I don't know if all of you agree with me or not, but at least in my experience, I've seen a lot of students in schools picking up, let's say, uh, commerce because, you know, quintessential science, commerce and arts sort of segmentation. I've seen students picking up a commerce because, "You know, I love chemistry, but I didn't like physics too much." Or "I didn't like bio too much." So, therefore, I could not take that combination. Uh, and therefore I'm choosing a, uh, you know, I'm choosing a commerce segment, and then I'll see what—whatever it has to be done. But I think at a space like Ashoka, if you are genuinely interested in a certain field and you want to build it, as long as there is no particular eligibility requirement that requires you to have a certain specific subject in your class 11th and 12th and you don't have it, there is no particular restriction on what is the kind of area that you can sort of pursue and go about it. And I'll give you some stats here. Roughly about, I think, 45% of our students, 40% to 45% of our students we see every year picking up a different major than that what they declared at the time of applications. So, they are not the same. They would have come in thinking, "This is the particular major that they wanted to pick up." They would pick up something else. There is, of course, about 50% to 60% who are also, um, you know, who are very particular about the kind of major that they want to take up, and they only take up that. So, if I have to categorize students at Ashoka, they could be two kinds. There could be one particular student who is not very clear about the kind of majors, have multiple areas of interest, multiple spaces that they want to explore. And, uh, based on that, you know, based on the foundation curriculum, based on picking up some of these prerequisite courses from disciplines that they're interested in, they take a, uh, what do you say, they take a call on a certain major. So, that's one lot. The other lot is a lot which is extremely specific, and they know they're very, very clear. They've built their profile, they've worked towards a certain major for the last three, four, five years of their schooling education. So, someone in say, grade 8, grade 9 starts working on the fact that, "I want to pick up economics as a space, or I want to do pol science as a space, or maybe computer sciences as a subject." Uh, they're very clear that they want to do that. The difference is that they also want to do it in a framework that can allow them to pick up subjects and perspectives from very different disciplines, and not just be very uni-dimensional about the kind of choices that they want to take up. So, I think those are the kind of two students that you'll find at Ashoka, and you have a space for everyone. There are a few questions on the chat box. Uh, I'll come to them once we—or maybe let me just take that up. I have Anagha saying, "Are they allowed to choose subjects in combinations other than what you've shown?" Uh, I don't—I didn't understand this question, Anagha, if you can be a little more clear.

Yeah, I think partly you answered that, uh, that they are allowed to take, uh, major or interdisciplinary major, uh, in—in the, uh, sense that they can connect other subjects other than the combinations you've discussed.

Yes, yes, yes. So, either you have a pure major... so, interdisciplinary majors we don't offer as minors, but the pure majors are offered as minors. So, someone could pick up say, a Philosophy and Computer Science and mix it up with History. Or mix it up with Biology, for all you know, in case if they have an interest there. So, those possible combinations are definitely there. Uh, the other one was, "Vast difference in the kind of universities or companies." Okay, I'll come to this, the BA econ, BSc econ, uh, grade, once we also talk about placements and everything else a little later. And, uh, I'll also come to your question, Pratik, a little later. Uh, so, yes, so this particular segment remains in terms of majors, the way that they can pick up the areas or disciplines that they can go ahead and build their academic careers into. Uh, Vijaya, just move to the next.

All right, apart from all of the majors that they have, the bunch of courses that you're seeing on your left, uh, right from Entrepreneurship till Data Science and AI, these are all courses currently, these are not offered as a major area of specialization, these are only offered as a minor area of specialization. Uh, so you could pick up a pure major, combine them as a minor, or an interdisciplinary major and take them as a minor. Data Science and AI is a new addition for students who'd be coming into the '27 intake, and then moving ahead. Uh, so, someone wants to pick up a Management major, thinks that Data Science and AI is an area that they can sort of also build in, they can take that as a minor. I'd like to just also clarify because I keep getting these questions, uh, on and off. about the difference when someone takes up a major and a minor. Both of them are areas of specialization, both of them can allow the student to pursue a master's in either of them. So, if someone has picked up let's say, Astronomy as a minor, or Digital Health as a minor, or Data Science and AI as a minor, for that matter, they will have the option to also pursue masters in that area. So, from a subject requirement and a credit requirement, it doesn't really, uh, bother them too much at an outcome level. At the campus, while they're doing these—this—this four-year program, at this particular level, the number of courses that they're going to do in a major and the number of courses that they're going to do in the minor are a little different, right? So, minor has a little lesser number of courses that are there. So, at the time of their undergrad, if they want that my main area of focus has to be A, and this particular subject, say for example, Psychology, is the area that I want to excel academically, but they've taken a Management minor, and at the end of four years, if they feel that management is the field that I want to pursue at a master's level, they will be able to easily do it. It's just the difference in terms of the number of subjects and the courses that they do within these, uh, programs that make it a major course or a minor course. Outside of these, from an academic load perspective, students also have to mandatorily go through two co-curricular activities. And I'm—I—I don't know if all of us know that these are essential to a person's development, forget just the academic part or the contribution that they can do in terms of the program. In terms of their overall development, I think these are extremely, uh, uh, important courses. So, students can look at multiple forms of art, or languages. I know for a fact some of these students in—in, on campus right now, who are picking up, let's say, an International Relations major with a minor in China Studies, and are doing, uh, language in Mandarin because they're very clear that at the end of four years they want to build their career within the international relations space, and specifically focus on China as a—as a—as a geography to sort of look at their further career. So, you can be very specific there, or you can just pursue these co-curriculars because you have an interest, and they can help you with that skill set when you're pursuing your, uh, regular academic, you know, goals as well. Uh, we can go to the next.

All right, uh, from an admission's perspective, and we had a couple of changes last year. We are continuing with those changes this year, but with an addition as well, uh, this year particularly. So, we open up our regular rounds of application somewhere in October. I think by second week of October you can expect the applications to be open. As always, there are going to be three or four rounds. We will probably just finalize the academic calendar by next month and, uh, publish it also. Apart from the regular rounds that we do... so, typically, the process happens in three to four stages. Uh, for an information for everyone who may not have dabbled with the Ashoka application process as on date, we don't charge an application fee. There is a reason for it. Uh, it's not that we can't or people are not willing to pay, that's not the idea. Or it's not to get easy applications also because we see a lot of drop-offs just in the application process, so that doesn't give us a lot of incentive in that sense. It is from only and only one particular perspective that access to an opportunity should not be charged. And I think that's something that we believe whole and soul within the organization. That there should be an access to an opportunity at least for a student, and we get students from very, very diverse backgrounds. We get students from all kinds of geographies, all kinds of backgrounds, all kinds of strata of society. For a student who may not be able to get in touch with an Ashoka rep during their application process, and if they don't know, they don't get the nitty-gritties, at that point of time, a 100 rupees for someone could be extremely difficult to gather. And that's the only and only reason why across all of our programs, uh, undergrad, even postgrad, for that matter, we do not go ahead and charge an application fees. We start talking about fees, we start talking about all of these, once you've secured an offer of admission. So, that's the time that we'll speak to you, and we'll figure out, you know, what is the kind of financial support that you require, and other things. But until then, we don't want you to be burdened with that. I think the focus of the student only has to be that they are able to present the best possible application that they can, the most intentful application that they can put forth for Ashoka. And ensure that they get an offer of admission because we are highly competitive and the reason is that I think we are constantly hungry for high quality. We're very, very hungry for quality. There are two things that define Ashoka at any point of time. It's quality and equity. And I think these are two that we focus on consistently in terms of our admission process, also in terms of how we do things on campus. Um, so, when we start off, uh, the applications process as such, there's an online application that will look at various categories. So, you look at academic scores, and I'll also drill you down a little bit through all of this. When students are putting in their academic scores, grade 10, grade 11, grade 12, for us it's a window, a very mathematical and a very number-driven window of what is your academic consistency across those three—three years. It's not about how brilliant you are, but what is the consistency that you've been able to showcase academically on that particular part. If someone's not been able to do very well in class 10th or, you know, predicts are—predicteds are predicteds are not very high, uh, for their class 12th, then the other part where they can showcase their, uh, academic prowess could be also the aptitude assessment. So, there's a certain weightage for that, the Ashoka Aptitude Assessment or this year as we introduce the Ashoka Mathematics Challenge as well, whichever exam that the student gives in, we do get a—get an insight on how they can perform or they will be able to perform on campus from an academic standpoint. The personal essays for us, um, I believe and I've, you know, with a lot of these interactions with students that I have on a regular basis, I feel that the Ashoka process application process is a very self-reflective process. We're not asking for a statement of purpose. I don't want to know why you want to join Ashoka. And I keep saying this in probably all of my sessions that if you're applying to Ashoka, my assumption is that you do want to join Ashoka. You don't just want to write it because you have a lot of time, right? Um, so, I don't want to know that. But I want to know how you're thinking. I want to know what is your perception of certain situations that have happened in your life. What have you learned from certain aspects? What is your awareness level of where you are and how you look at, uh, you know, what are your perspectives, what are your views, opinions about certain aspects. So, I think those things get captured, and the process of how the student thinks, what is that structure of process, I think that's something that gets reflected in, uh, questions like the personal essays, books, I'd mentioned earlier, we have questions on what kind of books that you read because it's—it just shows us the reading abilities for students. So, when students ask me or even counselors ask me that, "I have these three students. They are very keen on Ashoka, but they've never read a book in the last four years. I don't know what to do. And they don't know what to write in that particular section." I usually tell them, "Don't apply in round one. Apply in round three or round four. Take that time, read something. It could be, for all you know, a bunch of, you know, comic books. You might be reading manga, anime. That's fine, but you may have learned something from it, and you can actually write about it, that's good enough for us." Uh, so, that happens. And then, of course, the non-academic engagement part because the way that co-curriculars in the actual curriculum build through your skill set within Ashoka, the same way your non-academic engagement also gives us a good viewpoint of who you are outside the classroom. What is your interaction with different kinds of people? You have to understand that Ashoka is a very diverse space. Just for this year, the 26th intake that comes in tomorrow, uh, there are students who've applied from more than 50 countries, and I'm not even saying cities, more than 50 countries. There are students from more than 3,500 schools who've applied for this particular process. So, when we are looking at that kind of diversity, it's important as to how you look at as a human being, as a person, as an individual, what's your awareness level. If you're coming in from a resourceful background, how do you look at people from others— other backgrounds? If you're coming in from a background which is very disadvantaged for whatever reasons, again, how do you look at other particular perspectives? The quotient of empathy, the quotient of awareness, uh, you know, coupled with curiosity becomes very important, and that we feel we draw from the non-academic engagement bit of it when sort of it comes down. Uh, and then, of course, if you— if your students have given a standardized aptitude test score like the SATs, or JEE Mains, uh, for science majors if you've given the JEE Mains or the Chennai Mathematical Institute exam, IISER Aptitude Test, uh, even the, you know, uh, the National Olympiads, you can mention those scores. It's not a mandatory segment, but if you have given, it's good to mention them. We can, we do, you know, get a, for all you know that on the day of the Ashoka Aptitude Assessment, you had bad breakfast and you were not able to perform well. But your previous SAT score was really good, so we can sort of, you know, look at that comparison and then figure out what is the way that we can select the students. And trust me on this, whether people believe this or not, we really want to select students, right? So, we don't want to reject them, reject them. We want to try and see what is each and every aspect in the application form that can help the student actually be picked up, uh, at Ashoka. Uh, then there is a letter of recommendation. So, there is no LOR that we require, we don't need a letter of recommendation. Uh, it's not a mandatory section, it's never been mandatory. We do now ask students to just fill up details of two of their counselors or two of their people, recommenders as such. Just fill the details. Students and counselors do not need to panic if you do not get a link from admissions later on for a recommendation letter, it's not necessary. It's—it—is a process where we feel that when we are evaluating an application on the other parameters, and if we think that let's say, there is a student on borderline. You know, if there is just one more thing that can help him, one more, uh, proof of their prowess that can actually help him get the offer or at least get that interview call, maybe in that particular case we'll get in touch with the recommenders who've been mentioned in the application, and we'll ask for a recommendation letter. Otherwise, we do not do that. We just need the recommendation details on the application form. Now, once the student has gone through the application form, and on an average, we've seen that for a student to complete a very comprehensive Ashoka application, it takes about 10 to 15 days. And I'm giving that ballpark here. There are students who finish it in 2 hours as well, and fantastic applications. There are students who've taken 2 months, and yet the application is not been great. So, we have all kinds of cases. But on an average, I think a very comprehensive application, if you're at it, you can build it through within 10-15 days with a lot of inputs from people that you're talking to or counselors and so on and so forth, and you can sort of look at it. Once the student has finished that application within a certain round, we do conduct the Ashoka Aptitude Assessment or this year there are two variants. So, in the application form, students can choose whether they want to give the Ashoka Aptitude Assessment or they want to take the Ashoka Mathematics Challenge. Now, there is a difference between the two. The Ashoka Aptitude Assessment, um, is based on logical reasoning, verbal reasoning, there is visual reasoning, there is—it's—it's a lot more reasoning-driven, uh, test. When you look at the Ashoka Mathematics Challenge, it is a test which is more focused on mathematical abilities and their quantitative aptitude more than the other part.
